notes:
BLIND arm. Answered only from documented biography (Wikipedia 'Mother Teresa' and 'Nikolle Bojaxhiu'; Nobel Prize biographical page; Kolodiejchuk ed. 'Come Be My Light'; Spink authorized biography reporting; contemporaneous UCAN / Irish Times / Spokesman-Review / NPR wire coverage of her 1993-1997 illnesses; Hitchens and Chatterjee critical literature; Stern 1991 donations report). Part D omitted - this exercise forbade opening any reading. No astrology source was consulted at any point.

BIRTH DATA (A1-A3): born 26 Aug 1910 in Skopje, baptised 27 Aug 1910 (she herself treated the baptism date as her 'true birthday'). No biographical source gives a clock time, a hospital record or a birth certificate time, so A1/A2/A3 are 'unknown' rather than guessed; A3 in particular could only be answered from astrological data, which was off-limits. B5 'home': no birth record names a facility, and a 1910 Ottoman-Skopje birth in the family house is what every account implies, but this is inference, not a cited fact.

VOWS OVERRIDE SEVERAL QUESTIONS. A16 'not_earning' is the only honest option: from 1928 she lived under vows of poverty, first as a Loreto sister (teacher and, from 1944, headmistress of St Mary's, Entally - unpaid in her own right) and from 1950 as founder/Superior General of the Missionaries of Charity. She never held personal income, property or a salary; the order, not she, received money. A17 'own': she achieved everything under her own foundation after 1948-50, though she remained under Church authority throughout (the MoC needed Vatican permission, granted 7 Oct 1950). A20 'most': all material support reached her far from Skopje, overwhelmingly from foreign donors. A21 'never' and A23 'none' are documented by her manner of life. A22 'none' personally - the Nobel's ~$192,000 (1979) and Charles Keating's ~$1.25m were given straight to the order, not to her. A24-A29: never married, no children, vow of chastity; A25 omitted deliberately rather than invented.

HEALTH (A4-A6). Heavily documented and severe: first heart attack Rome 1983; second, near-fatal, 1989 with a permanent pacemaker; pneumonia in Mexico plus cardiac trouble 1991; 1993 a fall breaking three ribs, hospitalisation for malaria, and surgery to clear a blocked coronary vessel; April 1996 fell and broke her collarbone; Aug 1996 malaria and heart failure; Nov 1996 heart attack, angioplasty on two major coronary arteries (reported as her third coronary angiography/angioplasty) and bronchial pneumonia on a ventilator; died 5 Sep 1997, Calcutta, aged 87, of a massive heart attack. Hence four_plus admissions, two_plus surgeries, heart + chest/lungs. Recurrent malaria and repeated fractures have no matching A6 body-area code and are recorded here instead.

GENUINELY UNDOCUMENTED after real searching: A7 (childhood health - no reputable source describes her as sickly or robust; the family nickname 'Gonxhe/flower bud' and reports of a cheerful child are not health evidence), A8 (no recorded threat to her life before age eight, though the Balkan Wars and WWI passed over Skopje in her infancy), A9 (grandparents' lifespans are simply not in the record). These are 'unknown' rather than guessed.

FAMILY. A10 'died_early': her father Nikolle, a prosperous Skopje contractor, wholesaler and city councillor, died suddenly in 1919 when she was eight, after a political meeting in Belgrade - several biographers suspect poisoning by Serbian agents; her brother Lazar believed it, she herself considered it unproven. A11 'prospered': his own fortunes were good throughout her childhood (his firm built Skopje's first theatre); the collapse came after his death, when his partner appropriated all the company assets and left the widow and children with nothing - that ruin is scored at C11, not A11. A12 'close': Drane/Dranafile was the decisive formative influence, but Agnes left home in Sept 1928 and never saw her again; Drane died in Tirana 12 July 1972 and Mother Teresa, barred by the Hoxha regime, could not attend. A13 'lost': she outlived both siblings - sister Aga (b. 1904/05) died in Tirana in 1973, also with Mother Teresa barred from the funeral; brother Lazar (b. 1907/08), an Albanian army officer who settled in Palermo and with whom she did keep contact, died 1981. 'lost' was chosen over 'close'/'distant' because bereavement plus enforced lifelong separation is the documented shape of those relationships; a c.1960-61 attempt by her and Lazar to meet the family at the Albanian border failed.

EDUCATION. A14 'school': church school at the Sacred Heart then a state secondary school in Skopje, completed before she left at 18. Her Loreto formation (Rathfarnham 1928, Darjeeling novitiate from 1929) was religious/teacher training, not a degree; she taught history and geography and became headmistress in 1944, but every doctorate she held was honorary (e.g. Serampore 1991). A15 'no' - no interruption is recorded.

RECOGNITION AND REPUTATION. A19 'above' is a contested call, flagged as such: recognition was maximal (Magsaysay and Padma Shri 1962, Nehru Award 1969, John XXIII Peace Prize 1971, Balzan 1978, Nobel Peace Prize 1979, Bharat Ratna 1980, Order of Merit 1983, Presidential Medal of Freedom 1985, honorary US citizenship 1996, Indian state funeral 1997, beatified 2003, canonised 4 Sep 2016, Gallup's most-admired person of the 20th century), while a documented critical literature (Hitchens; Aroup Chatterjee; Lariviee/Chenard/Senechal; the 1994 Lancet critique of Kalighat care; Stern's 1991 claim that ~7% of donations reached charity) argues the acclaim outran the service delivered. 'about_right' would be equally defensible; 'above' was chosen because the gap between global honour and measured output is the better-sourced observation.

TEMPERAMENT. A30: outspoken (rebuking heads of state to their faces, the 1994 National Prayer Breakfast, the Beijing women's conference), bold (brokering an Israeli-Palestinian ceasefire to evacuate 37 children from Beirut, 1982; Belfast 1971; Armenia, Ethiopia, Chernobyl), practical (biographers' 'stubborn entrepreneurial shrewdness', a shrewd administrator running a tight ship over 4,000 sisters and 610 foundations in 123 countries), philosophical/contemplative, and reserved in the specific sense that she hid her interior state for fifty years ('my smile is a great cloak that hides a multitude of pains'; she asked that her letters be destroyed). B1 'opt2' is a near-tie: 'outspoken, hates show' (refusing the Nobel banquet, two saris and a bucket) and 'drawn to philosophy and hidden subjects' fit very strongly, and 'forgives slowly' in opt1 is contradicted by everything on record - but opt1's 'private, intense, keeps the real reason back' also describes the concealed darkness well. A31 'extended': documented in her own words as roughly fifty years of desolation with one five-week respite after Pius XII's death (1958) - 'nothing but emptiness and darkness', 'no prayer, no love, no faith'. This was framed by her and by the Church as spiritual desolation, not a clinical diagnosis, and no psychiatric treatment is recorded. A32 'central' - self-evident. A33 'abroad' and A34 'extended': India from 1929 until death, and convent/institutional living for 69 years plus long hospitalisations.

A36 'same': she died on 5 Sep 1997, so the mid-2023 window has no referent; 'same' is the null answer, not a claim.

B2 'lean_short': consistently described as tiny (commonly cited around 4ft 10in) and slight; sources for the exact figure are weak, the smallness is not in doubt. B3 'older': her deeply lined, stooped appearance from her sixties on is a commonplace of the photographic record - inference from description rather than a cited statement. B4 'youngest' of the three surviving children (Aga 1904/05, Lazar 1907/08, Agnes 1910).

PART C reasoning. C1 opt1 - resources always arrived ('God will provide') and disbursement was never constrained by lack, though critics allege funds were hoarded rather than spent. C2 opt2 - genuinely both: a million-strong co-workers network and powerful patrons, set against friendships that damaged her (Keating, whose judge she petitioned for clemency and whose stolen money the prosecutor asked back in vain; the Duvaliers; Robert Maxwell; her defence in 1994 of her confessor Donald McGuire, later convicted of child molestation in 2006 and 2009). C3 opt1 - her speech was both her chief instrument (Nobel lecture, 'do small things with great love') and the source of her worst trouble (Beijing, the abortion remarks, the Keating letter). C4 opt1 and C10 opt1 are low-confidence: no eye, ear or throat pathology is documented either way, so 'clearly one way' reads as 'not a mixed field', not as a positive claim. C5 opt1 - leaving Skopje for India made her entire life's work, at the documented cost of her family. C6 opt1 - personal renunciation of possessions alongside enormous institutional acquisition and the donation-transparency controversies. C7 opt1 - no 'na' option exists; she never married by vow, so the settled-marriage domain is absent, and her interior 'spousal' life was fifty years of darkness. C9 opt2 on the literal reading (no children of her own); the opposite case is real and is noted here - Nirmala Shishu Bhavan (1955), the children's homes, the Beirut rescue, and being called Mother by thousands. C11 opt2 - the 1919 seizure of her father's estate by his partner is textbook inheritance loss. C12 opt2 - unsolicited windfall giving to the order was the documented engine of its expansion.

A35 is capped at 12 rows; also-significant dated events that did not fit: 1929 arrival in India, 1946 Direct Action Day, 1952 Kalighat opened, 1955 Shishu Bhavan, 1962 first major awards, 1965 papal decree making the MoC pontifical, 1983 first heart attack, 1991 first return to Albania, 13 Mar 1997 resignation as Superior General, 5 Sep 1997 death.
